Question nine. What is ROC-AUC, and when is PR-AUC preferred? The ROC curve, for receiver operating characteristic, plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold. The AUC is the area under the curve: point five is chance, one is perfect. Here it's point nine four. The PR curve plots precision against recall, and its area here is only point four five. Same model, same scores, but keep only as many negatives as positives. ROC-AUC barely moves. PR-AUC jumps to point nine four. The false positive rate divides by every negative, so a flood of easy ones flatters the ROC curve. When positives are rare, PR-AUC is the honest one. Question ten. How do you handle class imbalance? Start by ignoring accuracy: calling every case negative is already ninety-eight percent accurate. Weight the rare class in the loss, and at a threshold of point five, recall goes from twenty-seven percent to eighty-six, while precision falls from sixty-seven to eleven. Or move the threshold, or resample, and judge the result by PR-AUC or F one.

Question eleven. What is model calibration? Whether a score means what it says: of the cases scored point eight, about eighty percent should be positive. The plain model sits near the diagonal. The weighted one doesn't: of the cases it scores around point eight five, under nine percent are positive. The weights bought recall and broke the probabilities. Fit a calibration on held-out data, with Platt scaling or isotonic regression, and it's back on the line.
